segments.narration: A thorn hedge once cut India clean in half. Four thousand kilometres of it, ordered joined up in 1869, Himalayas down to the Bay of Bengal.
It was there to tax salt. Indian plum, babool, prickly pear, grown nearly four metres high and four metres thick in places.
Over fourteen thousand men patrolled it at its peak, through more than seventeen hundred customs posts. All that, to stop smuggled salt.
Then on 1 April 1879, they dropped it. And a barrier the size of a country simply fell out of the history books.
In 1998 a researcher named Roy Moxham found what's left: one low earth embankment in Etawah district.

verdicts.claim: The British Inland Customs Line was ordered connected in 1869 into a continuous barrier of 4,030 kilometres running from the Himalayas to Orissa near the Bay of Bengal.
verdicts.note: 100% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The line existed to enforce the salt tax and collect sugar duty, and was built from thorny species including Indian plum, babool and prickly pear, reaching 3.7 metres high and 4.3 metres thick in places.
verdicts.note: 91% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Staff on the customs line peaked at 14,188 men in 1872, and there were 1,727 customs posts in 1869 to 1870.
verdicts.note: 86% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 5 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The line was abandoned on 1 April 1879 after Britain took control of salt production, and standard histories of the period largely omitted it.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: maintenance stopped in 1878 and the line was abandoned on 1 April 1879 after Britain took control of salt production; standard histories of the period largely omitted it and it was little known in Britain or India.

verdicts.claim: In 1998 Roy Moxham located a small raised embankment in Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, which may be all that remains of the hedge.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: Moxham found a passing mention in 1995, then in 1998 located a small raised embankment in Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, which may be all that remains. Live History India corroborates the Etawah find. His occupation is not stated in the cited sources, so the narration calls him a researcher.

candidates.why: Leads on the absurd geography: a hedge as a national border.

candidates.text: Fourteen thousand men guarded a hedge made of thorns
candidates.why: Leads on the manpower, which makes the scale of enforcement land.

candidates.text: Britain taxed salt with four thousand kilometres of thorns
candidates.why: Leads on the purpose and the length together, closing the why too early.

choice.reason: It is the only candidate that leaves the purpose unexplained, and a hedge working as a border is instantly absurd without any knowledge of the Raj.
